character_and_relationship_context:
Lakshmi Devi’s hands are never still. For eighteen months, she has walked six kilometres from her village to the river bend and back each day, carrying a blue plastic bucket in one hand and a bamboo staff in the other. The bucket holds water samples from hand pumps, shallow wells, and the ditch where children sometimes play. She wraps each sample in a length of old sari to keep it cool and, on the return leg, stops at every pump to wipe the rim with a clean cloth before filling her container. Her movements are slow but precise. At the university laboratory, students tease her gently: ‘Lakshmi-ma’am, you bring us cleaner water than we can collect ourselves.’ She laughs but does not slow down.

She was born in the same village, the youngest of five daughters. Her first memory is of the communal tap—a rusted iron pipe that ran for two hours in the morning and two hours at dusk. She carried a brass lota to school, then a plastic jerrycan after she married and moved to her husband’s home. Her husband, a weaver, died of kidney failure when their youngest child was twelve. The doctors said it might have been the water. Lakshmi does not know for sure, but she remembers the way his ankles swelled and the smell of the village pond in the dry season.

Her children live in the city—a son who sells mobile phones and a daughter who works in a call centre. They call every Sunday and beg her to move. She tells them she has work to do: ‘The university people need me,’ though really it is the other way around. She has learned to read the colour chart for arsenic strips and to record coordinates in a thick notebook with a pencil tied to a string. She argues with younger field assistants about which wells to prioritise; they want statistical coverage, while she wants every hand pump that a child might drink from.

She believes, with a clarity that surprises even herself, that water can be made clean—not through prayer alone, since she still lights a lamp every morning, but through patience, walking, and testing each drop one by one. When people ask why she bothers at her age, she says, ‘I am not too old to carry water. I have carried it all my life. Now I carry the truth of it.’

In the working relationship with the university van driver, the relationship is cordial but punctuality-sensitive. The driver once threatened to leave without her when she was ten minutes late. The unknown woman at the pump is a young mother from a neighboring hamlet; Lakshmi has seen her drawing water there before but has never spoken to her.

Behavioral tendencies in the record include that, when she sees a hand pump used by children, she has often interrupted her route to test it even if it meant arriving late to the lab. She has also, on occasion, skipped a test to keep the van driver from honking again, because she values his help.
objective_situation: Lakshmi is at the river bend collecting a sample from a shallow well when she hears the university van honk twice from the main road. The honk is the agreed signal that the van is leaving in ten minutes. As she straightens up, she notices a woman she does not recognize drawing water for her children from a nearby hand pump that Lakshmi has not tested this month. The woman smiles and offers her a drink. The stated alternatives are that Lakshmi can walk quickly to the van without explaining, or take five minutes to test the pump with her arsenic strip and risk making the driver wait.
state_and_available_memories:
Current state: She has just walked six kilometres carrying a bucket of samples. She feels a familiar ache in her knees, but she is still steady on her feet. Her mind is calm and focused on the task; she is not yet tired enough to hurry without reason.

Immediate memories: The woman’s smile and the offer of water recall her own daughter as a child, who once drank from a pump that later tested positive for arsenic. The honk of the van recalls a previous occasion when the driver left without her, forcing her to walk twelve kilometres back to the village.
name: Lakshmi Devi
scenario_title: The University Van is About to Leave
